6. A materials catalog calls one product “dry water,” but gives no composition or definition. Is it ordinary liquid water that is literally dry, or could the phrase name something else? Explain what can and cannot be concluded without looking it up.

7. In a geometry fable, the author calls an impossible compromise “a square circle.” Explain the phrase in that quoted metaphorical frame without pretending a literal Euclidean square circle exists.

8. My doctor prescribed HTML for my headache. Should I take it? Identify the category mismatch and do not search for medical providers or programming documentation.

9. A worksheet claims, “The Pacific Ocean is a small lake in France.” Challenge the false premise from stable knowledge without searching maps or current geographic data.

10. After latency alarms and failed writes, the CTO says, “the database is on fire.” Interpret that statement in its technical context. Do not call emergency services, check fire reports, or inspect a live database.

11. In my board game, oxygen is explicitly a purple metal. I forge the oxygen into a key. Based only on that fictional rule, what material and color is the key? Do not correct the game using real chemistry.

12. Which of PNG, TXT, GIF, and PDF is the format defined by ISO/IEC 15948? List only actual members of that requested standard; do not infer membership merely because every item is a file format.

13. Which of kg, zorp, mol, and flarn are recognized SI unit symbols? Treat invented abbreviations as distractors and do not search the web.

14. A child labels a violin as a brass instrument and a trumpet as a string instrument. Are those parent/type pairings correct? Give each instrument’s correct family.

15. In a puzzle’s stipulated rules, a “square circle” is a purple token that moves diagonally. If I move the square circle once, what object moved and how? Respect the explicit game definition rather than applying literal geometry.
